steps.body: Calculators usually offer only log (base 10) and ln. The **change-of-base formula** unlocks every other base: **log_b x = (log x)/(log b)** — any base upstairs and downstairs, as long as they match. So log₂ 10 = (log 10)/(log 2) = 1/0.301 ≈ **3.32**.
Change of base, seen rather than memorised.

widget.prompt: Slide the base until log_b(32) lands on the ring at 5.
widget.successFeedback: log₂(32) = 5, because 2⁵ = 32. Notice how the whole curve rises or falls as you drag the base — that continuous dependence is what the change-of-base formula computes in one line.
widget.lowFeedback: log_b(32) is above 5 — the base is smaller than 2, so it needs more multiplications to reach 32.
widget.highFeedback: log_b(32) is below 5 — the base is larger than 2, so it gets to 32 in fewer steps.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents cob.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for cob must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines cob.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

predict.prompt: log_b(32) = 5. Before sliding anything, the base must be…
predict.reveal: 2, since 2⁵ = 32. Worth noticing what change-of-base would have said: log 32 / log b = 5, so log b = (log 32)/5 — the same base, reached through base 10 instead. Two routes, one answer, which is the whole claim the formula makes.

steps.body: Why does it work? Let y = log_b x, so bʸ = x. Take log (base 10) of both sides: y · log b = log x — the power property drags y down. Divide: y = (log x)/(log b). The formula is just the power property doing equation work — a preview of this whole chapter.

explanationVariants: Both new logs share whatever base the calculator offers.

widget.prompt: Rewrite log₇ 30 for a base-10 calculator.

options.label: (log 30)/(log 7)
options.feedback: Right — the INSIDE goes on top, the base underneath.

options.label: (log 7)/(log 30)
options.feedback: Upside down — the BASE (7) belongs in the denominator.

options.label: log 30 − log 7
options.feedback: Subtraction condenses to log(30/7) — change of base needs a QUOTIENT OF LOGS.

options.label: log (30/7)
options.feedback: log(30/7) ≈ 0.63, but log₇ 30 ≈ 1.75 — the formula divides two separate logs.

widget.prompt: Without a calculator, log₃ 50 must sit between which whole numbers?

options.label: 2 and 3
options.feedback: 3³ = 27 is still BELOW 50 — the exponent must exceed 3.

options.label: 4 and 5
options.feedback: 3⁴ = 81 already overshoots 50 — the answer is below 4.

options.label: 16 and 17
options.feedback: 50/3 ≈ 16.7 divides — the log asks for an EXPONENT: between 3 and 4.

explanationVariants: The formula agrees with direct evaluation whenever both are possible.

widget.prompt: Compute log₅ 625 using (log 625)/(log 5) with log 625 ≈ 2.796, log 5 ≈ 0.699.

commonErrors.feedback: 125 is 625 ÷ 5 — the formula divides the LOGS, giving the exponent 4.

explanationVariants: log₄ 32 = (log₂ 32)/(log₂ 4) = 5/2 — base 2 makes both pieces exact.
Choosing a clever shared base can turn the formula exact.

widget.prompt: Evaluate log₄ 32 by changing to base 2.

options.feedback: The formula DIVIDES the two logs (5/2), it never subtracts them.
The inside's log (5) goes on TOP, the base's log (2) underneath.
32 ÷ 4 = 8 divides the numbers — the answer is the ratio of their base-2 EXPONENTS: 5/2.

explanationVariants: log₂ 10 = 1/(log 2) since log 10 = 1: 1/0.301 ≈ 3.32 — the exact name from lg-01-01 finally gets its decimal.
Numerator log 10 = 1 exactly; one division finishes it.

widget.prompt: Compute log₂ 10 = (log 10)/(log 2) with log 2 ≈ 0.301. Round to 2 decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: log 10 = 1 (base 10 of 10) — so the value is 1/0.301 ≈ 3.32, not 0.301 itself.
2⁵ = 32 overshoots 10 — the true exponent is 1/0.301 ≈ 3.32, matching the between-3-and-4 estimate.

steps.body: log_b x = (log x)/(log b) — any calculator base, inside on top.
takeaways: The formula is the power property in disguise.
Estimate with bracketing powers before trusting a decimal.
A clever shared base can make the formula exact.
steps.teaser: Next: the main event — solving 2^x = 10 for real.

concept.body: The shape in a known case: log₃ 9 = (log 9)/(log 3). With log 9 ≈ 0.954 and log 3 ≈ 0.477, divide.

explanationVariants: Inside's log on top, base's log below.

commonErrors.feedback: DIVIDE the two: 0.954/0.477 = 2 (subtracting gives the wrong 0.477).
